https://english.radio.cz/govt-approves-p.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Govt approves pay transparency, platform work bills Facebook Twitter The Czech government on Monday approved an amendment to the Labour Code introducing EU pay transparency rules and a bill regulating platform work. Under the new pay rules, unjustified gender pay gaps of five percent or more will have to be corrected within six months. Job applicants will also have to be informed about pay and bonuses before signing a contract. The platform work bill will allow workers to be classified as employees if their work meets employment criteria. It also tightens rules on illegal work and requires human oversight of algorithms. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/25/the-.text: After more than four years of war between Russia and Ukraine, technology and spending on military equipment have evolved significantly.A number of Russian drones have been detected flying over European Union territory. There have been incursions into Poland and Bulgaria although, according to a CIA report, the situation could become more complicated.The latest information from the CIA has made it clear that there is a risk of Russian drone attacks on Spain, France or Italy launched from containers on ships belonging to the shadow fleet in the Mediterranean. So, what kind of drones is the Russian army using? According to the latest information from the Ukrainian military, it goes far beyond the use of Iranian-made Shahed drones.In the early hours of 27 August, Ukrainian air defences shot down or neutralised 233 Russian targets in a single night-time bombardment. Among them were 258 attack drones, two Oniks anti-ship missiles and several Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles.According to the Ukrainian Air Force, around a third of those drones are jet-powered, while the rest are a mix of Shahed-type drones, Gerbera systems and Banderol missiles, as well as decoys.That mix gives a fairly accurate picture of the state of Russia’s unmanned arsenal at this stage of the war: it is no longer based on a single model but on a whole family of systems performing different roles, from flooding the sky with cheap swarms to punching through at more than 500 kilometres per hour.Part of the explanation lies in cost. Firing a million-dollar interceptor at a drone worth between €25,000-40,000 (€21,000-35,000) is unsustainable in the long run and that imbalance is precisely what Moscow is exploiting by launching waves capable of exhausting far more expensive air-defence systems with its drones, as well as with more conventional weapons.Russia’s industrial base and the production raceThe bulk of this drone fleet comes from the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, some 1,200 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. The complex covers more than 2.8 million square metres and it is estimated that around 15% of its facilities are devoted, directly or indirectly, to war production.There, composite fuselages are moulded, engines are manufactured, onboard electronics are assembled and completed parts are stored.Ukrainian strikes on the complex have forced Russia to move much of that chain underground.A Ukrainian open-source analyst estimates that around 42,000 square metres of underground space have already been built at Alabuga, the equivalent of six football pitches.According to Russian media cited by 'The Economist', daily production of Geran-2 drones already exceeds 100 units, with plans to reach 500 a day. Geran-2 drones are the systems better known as the Shahed-136.In terms of overall volume, estimates vary by source but point in the same direction. The Centre for Strategic and International Studies calculated that in March 2026 Russia was producing around 5,500 drones a month, while Ukrainian military intelligence put August output at around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones and some 2,800 Geran-2 a month.In March of that same year, according to a report cited by Euronews, Russia had launched 6,462 Shahed-type drones and related attack and decoy systems, of which 4,186 were Shahed-type Geran-2 attack drones, an average of 208 launches a day – a pace that on some days rose to more than 900 drones.Geran-2: The drone that saturates Ukrainian defencesThis is the model that has underpinned most attacks since 2022. Designed in Iran, Russia manufactures its own version at Alabuga under the Geran-2 designation.Manufacturer: HESA / Shahed Aviation Industries (Iran); Russian version assembled at Alabuga under the Geran-2 designation.Dimensions: 3.5 metres long with a 2.5-metre wingspan.Weight: Around 200 kilograms.Propulsion: Mado MD-550 four-stroke piston engine of about 50 horsepower, with a rear propeller.Cruising speed: Around 185 km/h.Range: Between 1,000 and 2,500 kilometres depending on the version; the Russian variant with a reinforced 90-kg warhead has its range cut to around 1,000 kilometres.Explosive payload: Between 30 and 50 kilograms in the standard version, with a casing that combines conventional explosives with thermobaric material and metal fragmentation elements.Estimated cost: Between $20,000-50,000 (€17,000-43,000) per unit.In service since: September 2022.Ukrainian interception rate: Estimated at between 65% and 85% according to Global Military.Geran-3, Geran-4 and Geran-5: The race for speedAs Ukrainian interceptors have improved, Russia has been replacing propellers with jet engines. The leap has taken place in three stages.The first, the Geran-3, based on the Shahed-238, reused the Geran-2 fuselage with an added turbojet. It reached speeds of between 300 and 370 km/h and had an operational range of close to 1,000 kilometres, with a combined thermal and fragmentation warhead of around 50 kilograms.Ukrainian intelligence documented dozens of foreign components in its wreckage, many of them from US manufacturers, as well as Chinese and European parts.The Geran-4 followed with an entirely redesigned fuselage rather than a simple adaptation. Its dimensions remain similar to those of the original Shahed – about 3.5 metres long with a 3-metre wingspan – but with integrated fixed wings to reduce drag.According to specialist analysis, it cruises at between 300-350 km/h, with peaks of up to 500 km/h, flies at 4,000 to 5,000 metres and delivers a 50-kilogram warhead at a range of between 450 and 850 kilometres.In practice, however, Russia has managed to stretch that figure: flying at high altitude to cut fuel consumption, a Geran-4 recorded a flight of around 960 kilometres on 28 August 2026, a distance that brings almost the whole of Ukrainian territory within range. Its cost is put at between $85,000-120,000 (€74,000-105,000) per unit.The Geran-5 is the most recent variant. According to an analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, it can reach up to 600 km/h, has a range of about 950 kilometres and a payload of around 90 kilograms; German-made transistors have been found in its remains. Both models are powered by the TF-TJ2000A engine.The impact on Ukrainian defences has been significant. In March 2026 Ukraine was intercepting more than 90% of the drones launched against its territory; by June, with Geran jet drones deployed on a large scale, that rate had fallen to just over 50%. Kyiv responded with its own jet-powered interceptors, such as the Alexa Spatium, which entered service on 21 August 2026.Gerbera: The decoy that turned into a weaponOriginally conceived as a cheap decoy to saturate radar screens alongside real Geran-2 drones, the Gerbera model has been steadily gaining its own offensive capability.Manufacturer identified by Ukrainian intelligence: JSC Alabuga Skywalker Technology Co.Estimated cost: Around $10,000 (€8,000) per unit.Dimensions: 2 metres long with a 2.5-metre wingspan.Maximum speed: Up to 160 km/h.Range (decoy version): between 300 and 600 kilometres.Ceiling: Up to 3,000 metres.In service since: July 2024.Recent evolution: Gerbera drones manufactured at Alabuga, hitherto used as decoys, are being fitted with high-explosive fragmentation warheads produced by the company Bazalt and KZ-6 charges.Lancet: Precision munitions against armoured vehiclesUnlike the Shahed and Geran drones, designed for long-range strikes, the Lancet is a short-range weapon intended to hit specific frontline targets such as artillery, radar systems or armoured vehicles.Manufacturer: ZALA Aero Group, part of the Kalashnikov concern.Unveiled: June 2019, at the ARMY-2019 military fair in Moscow.Variants: Izdeliye 51, with 60 minutes of endurance and a 5-kilogram warhead, and Izdeliye 52, lighter, with 40 minutes and a 3-kilogram warhead, the version most widely used at the front.Maximum take-off weight: Up to 12 kilograms.Range: Up to 40 kilometres in the standard version; a model detected in 2025 with a redesigned antenna system extends that range.Speed: cruising speed of 80 to 110 km/h, with a dive impact speed of up to 300 km/h, according to WikiTanks.Guidance: GLONASS-based inertial navigation in the approach phase, with real-time electro-optical correction on the final target, according to Defensa.Warhead: high explosive or fragmentation; in August 2025 Russia began replacing the standard KZ-6 charge with a PTM-3 anti-tank mine, increasing the explosive load from 1.5 to 1.8 kilograms at the cost of reduced armour penetration, according to UNITED24 Media.It is worth noting that social networks have circulated claims of a variant called Lancet XXL, with a warhead equivalent to 20 kilograms of TNT and a range of 200 kilometres, powered by an internal combustion engine instead of the usual electric motor.However, this version has not been officially confirmed either by ZALA Aero or by the Russian Defence Ministry.Orlan-10: The eyes of the Russian artilleryThis is not an attack drone but a reconnaissance platform whose main role is to correct artillery fire and monitor troop movements.Manufacturer: Special Technology Centre, based in Saint Petersburg.Maximum take-off weight: 16.5 kilograms.Payload: up to 6 kilograms, including day and thermal cameras and, in its attack variant, small bombs.Endurance: around 18 hours.Range: between 120 and 600 kilometres depending on operating mode.Speed: cruising speed of 110 km/h and maximum of 150 km/h.Ceiling: 5,000 metres.Estimated cost: between $87,000-120,000 (€76,000-105,000).Production: more than 1,000 units built, in 11 different variants.Tactical use: typically deployed in groups of two or three, sharing reconnaissance, electronic warfare and data relay roles.Orion: Russia’s attempt to mimic the MQ-9 ReaperThis is the most ambitious combat drone in the Russian arsenal, although serial production was slow to ramp up and it has never played as prominent a role as the Shaheds.Manufacturer: Kronshtadt Group, based in Dubna.Category: medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) UAV, with a configuration similar to the US MQ-9 Reaper.Weight: around one tonne.Maximum speed: 200 km/h.Ceiling: 7,500 metres.Endurance: up to a full day of operation.Range: 250 kilometres, extendable via satellite link.Armament: up to four air-to-surface missiles with warheads of between 7 and 20 kilograms; it carries the guided X-50 missile, developed specifically for this platform, and more recently the S8000 Banderol cruise missile, with a maximum speed of 650 km/h, cruising at 560 km/h, and a range of 500 kilometres.Estimated cost: around $7 million (€6 million) per unit.Technological dependence: according to Ukrainian intelligence, much of its electronics come from US and other Western manufacturers despite sanctions.Combat history: Syria (2019), Ukraine (2022).Fibre-optic FPV drones: immune to electronic warfareThe latest development is not about range but about electromagnetic stealth. Because they are physically connected by cable to the operator, these drones emit no radio signal that can be jammed or detected.First known Russian model: Kniaz Vandal Novgorodsky, developed by the volunteer tech group Ushkuinik and deployed around August 2024 in the Kursk region.Cable length: between 5 and 20 kilometres in typical models, with some prototypes reaching up to 50 kilometres.Operational range: between 20 and 30 kilometres for Russian quadcopters, with a hit rate of close to 80% at a distance of 20 kilometres.Payload: up to 2 or 3 kilograms in the most common tactical models."Sleeper" variant: fitted with a module called Gibernator that allows the drone to go into hibernation for weeks without emitting any signal, to ambush targets near key objectives, and which, according to its chief engineer, can remain on standby for up to a month in summer.Typical targets: logistics hubs, rear-area positions, vehicles and areas close to the front line.The Russian army has a multitude of drones at its disposal and some of them have a range of up to 1,000 kilometres, which means that the CIA’s estimates may in fact underestimate the threat of a possible attack on Spain, France or Italy from the Mediterranean.From a ship in the shadow fleet in the Mediterranean, the Russian army could launch Geran-2, Geran-3, Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones, all capable of carrying an explosive payload to targets at almost 1,000 kilometres.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmj4.text: Image source, Naomi-Scherbel Ball/BBC Image caption, Serhii Beskrestnov said "people have already died" due to lack of warnings about incoming missile attacks By Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent in Kyiv Published 19 October 2026, 19:23 BST Updated 1 hour ago Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died." The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing. The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week , as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows. Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence. On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter." Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause. "We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles." But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue. "This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not." He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack." However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component." Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications. Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h). This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas. Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement. Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine. He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'." Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems. He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step. "We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink." On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing." Figure caption, Watch: Moment Ukrainian soldier lifted to safety by drone Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing. "I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday. Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system." The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response. A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine. The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country. Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park cafÃ© in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity". https://hvg.hu/zhvg/20261109_kornyezetve.text: Azt szeretnék, hogy a kormány mielőbb bocsátsa társadalmi vitára a törvénytervezetet, és az Országgyűlés még az idén fogadja el az új klímatörvényt. Nyílt levélben fordultak környezetvédelmi civil szervezetek a miniszterelnökhöz, mert attól tartanak, hogy a kormány klímatörvény-tervezetének csúszása miatt az idén már nem marad elég idő a társadalmi vitára és a törvény elfogadására – közölte a Magyar Természetvédők Szövetsége hétfőn az MTI-vel. A közleményben felidézték: Magyar Péter miniszterelnök augusztus 23-án bejelentette, majd augusztus 27-én az Országgyűlésben is megerősítette, hogy ősszel benyújtják az új klímatörvényt. A civilek bizakodva fogadták, hogy a kormány is dolgozik az új szabályozáson. Mint kiemelték: november elején a kormány tervezete még nem nyilvános, és a széles körű társadalmi vitára bocsátás menetrendje sem ismert. A levél aláírói attól tartanak, hogy így az év végéig nem marad elég idő a tervezet érdemi megvitatására és parlamenti elfogadására. „Köztudott, hogy a kapcsolódó egyre sürgetőbb intézkedések megtervezése és megvalósítása, a hazai és EU-források felhasználása megalapozott szabályozás nélkül nem sikerülhet, ezért minden késedelmes nap sok hónapos csúszást okozhat a felkészülésben” – írták a közleményben. A korábbi klímatörvényt tavaly semmisítette meg az Alkotmánybíróság, és arra kötelezte a kormányt, hogy idén június 30-ig alkosson új jogszabályt. A kormányzatot ebben megelőzték a civilek, akik már tavaly elkezdtek dolgozni egy koncepción, amely idén júliusban elkészült , és amit az új kormány is jó szívvel fogadott . Megnyomták „a Send gombot”, és olyan átfogó kerettörvényt küldött a kormánynak közel 200 civil szervezet, amelyet akár már másnap be lehet nyújtani a parlamentnek, miután már túl vannak vele a szakmai és társadalmi egyeztetéseken is. Ha mégsem tart rá igényt az új kormány – mivel maga is dolgozik hasonlón –, az átfogó kerettörvény-tervezet akkor is jó szolgálatot tesz majd: lehet mihez mérni a várhatóan ősszel megszülető végleges jogszabályt. A több mint 200 szervezet összefogásával készült tervezet célja, hogy Magyarország ne csak az üvegházhatású gázok kibocsátását csökkentse, hanem felkészüljön a klímaváltozás egyre súlyosabb következményeire is. Az Alkotmánybíróság tavalyi döntése is átfogó szabályozást sürgetett, amely a kibocsátáscsökkentés mellett az alkalmazkodást és az ország ellenálló képességének növelését is rendezi – emlékeztet a mostani közlemény. A civil szervezetek hangsúlyozzák, hogy a törvény tartalma legalább olyan fontos, mint a mielőbbi elfogadása. Egyértelmű kibocsátáscsökkentési célokat, ötéves karbonköltségvetéseket, független tudományos tanácsot és önálló klímavédelmi hatóságot javasolnak, valamint a kormányzati kötelezettségek jogi számonkérhetőségét. Az alkalmazkodásnak a kibocsátáscsökkentéssel azonos súlyt kell kapnia, konkrét állami és önkormányzati feladatokkal, biztos pénzügyi háttérrel – ezt szolgálhatná a kibocsátáskereskedelmi bevételekből finanszírozott klímaalap is. A szervezetek szerint az ország ellenálló képességének erősítéséhez a mezőgazdaság, a vízgazdálkodás, az energetika és más ágazatok szabályait is felül kell vizsgálni. Abban bíznak, hogy a kormány mielőbb társadalmi vitára bocsátja a törvénytervezetét, és az Országgyűlés még az idén megtárgyalhatja és elfogadhatja az új klímatörvényt. A nyílt levelet a Green Policy Center, az Energiaklub Szakpolitikai Intézet, az Éghajlatvédelmi Szövetség, a Greenpeace Magyarország, a Levegő Munkacsoport, a Magyar Madártani és Természetvédelmi Egyesület, a Magyar Természetvédők Szövetsége, a Naphimnusz Teremtésvédelmi Egyesület, a Reflex Környezetvédő Egyesület és a WWF Magyarország képviselői írták alá. Gajdos László élő környezetért felelős miniszter a múlt héten a HVG érdeklődésére egy háttérbeszélgetésen megerősítette, hogy első olvasatban tárgyalta a klímatörvényt a kormány. A tárcavezető szerint a klímatörvény tervezete vaskos, nem olyan, mint az előző kormányé volt. Kérdésünkre, hogy mennyire használták fel a civilek javaslattervezetét, azt mondta, nagymértékben arra épül az általuk kidolgozott javaslat. Gajdos azt ígérte, hogy hamarosan kikerül társadalmi egyeztetésre is. Egy fakivágásos háttérbeszélgetésen beszélt az új klímatörvényről a miniszter a HVG-nek. Azt mondta, hogy a tervezet már benn van a rendszerben, és hamarosan nyilvános lesz. Budapesten és Pest megyében több helyszínen zajlanak elfogások és házkutatások egy embercsempész ügyben.
